patient.name: Harold Watkins
patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral hand and foot weakness and numbness for 3 years, slow progression, family told to see a specialist
patient.hpi: Harold Watkins is a 56-year-old electrician with a 3-year history of progressive bilateral hand and foot weakness and sensory loss. He has had extensive prior workup attributed his neuropathy to 'mixed diabetic and toxic neuropathy from electrical work' — both of which his current neurologist is questioning. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 5 years ago (current HbA1c 7.8%) and his prior physicians attributed his neuropathy to this. He works as an industrial electrician but denies any significant solvent or heavy metal exposures confirmed by occupational health records. He notes that his father was 'basically in a wheelchair at 60 from leg weakness' though he never received a diagnosis. He has two adult children, one of whom (son, age 31) recently complained to his own physician about numb feet. He denies alcohol use. Over the past 6 months, he notes episodic carpal-tunnel-like pain at both wrists that he attributes to his job. He has been wearing bilateral wrist splints. A recent EMG at an outside institution was interpreted as 'length-dependent diabetic axonal neuropathy consistent with history.' He presents now because a podiatry colleague noticed extremely high arches on foot examination and referred him, stating 'this doesn't look like diabetic feet.' He also has prominent muscle wasting in his hands (interossei and thenar) and what he calls 'claw hands' that he attributes to grip fatigue from electrical work. He takes no immune-modulating medications.
pmh: Carpal tunnel syndrome (bilateral, wearing wrist splints — possibly iatrogenic diagnosis)
patient.review_of_systems: Positive: bilateral hand and foot weakness/numbness, high-arched feet (lifelong), hand muscle wasting, bilateral wrist pain (carpal tunnel-attributed). Negative: bowel/bladder dysfunction, vision changes, hearing loss, ataxia, falls.

family_history: Father: bilateral leg weakness, needed wheelchair at age 60, never formally diagnosed. Son (31): recently developed bilateral foot numbness. Mother: type 2 diabetes. No known family neuropathy diagnosis.

social_history.note: Industrial electrician (30 years). Married. Non-smoker. Non-drinker (alcohol). No illicit drugs. Occupational health review: no significant heavy metal or solvent exposure documented.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II-XII intact. No facial weakness.
neurological_exam.motor: Hand intrinsics (interossei, lumbricals): 3/5 bilaterally — SEVERE INTRINSIC WASTING. Thenar and hypothenar eminences bilaterally atrophied. Finger extensors 4/5 bilaterally. Wrist extensors 4+/5. Biceps 5/5. Foot dorsiflexors 3/5 bilaterally. Plantar flexors 4/5. Hip flexors 5/5.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced vibration at great toes (4 seconds) and ankles (8 seconds). Reduced pinprick in stocking distribution to mid-shin and glove distribution to mid-hand. Reduced light touch at fingertips bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 1+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 1+ bilaterally. Patellar 1+ bilaterally. Achilles ABSENT bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild finger-nose dysmetria from hand weakness. Gait with bilateral steppage.
neurological_exam.gait: BILATERAL STEPPAGE — foot drop bilateral. Inverted champagne bottle calves visible. Stork legs appearance.
neurological_exam.special_tests: PES CAVUS high arch bilateral (arch 48 mm). HAMMER TOES bilateral. CLAW HANDS (distal phalanges extended at DIP, flexed at PIP — intrinsic minus hand from interosseous wasting). No Babinski. No Tinel's at wrist (despite carpal tunnel diagnosis at outside institution).

specialized_test.test_type: Nerve Conduction Study and EMG (repeat, in-house)

report.summary: REPEAT NCS/EMG with attention to VELOCITY PATTERN, not just amplitudes. CRITICAL FINDING MISSED IN PRIOR STUDY: Motor conduction velocities are uniformly very slow throughout (28-34 m/s) — characteristic of CMT1 hereditary demyelinating neuropathy, NOT diabetic axonal neuropathy. Prior NCS interpretation as 'diabetic axonal' was incorrect because amplitudes were low (consistent with both), but velocities were markedly slow (diagnostic of CMT1, not diabetes).

motor.note: Velocity <30 m/s — CMT1 range; diabetic neuropathy would have velocities >38 m/s

motor.flag: SEVERELY SLOW and low amplitude (chronic axonal loss superimposed)

nerve_conduction_studies.note_on_prior_study: Prior NCS report labeled this as 'length-dependent axonal diabetic neuropathy' — this interpretation overlooked the velocity pattern. Diabetic axonal neuropathy: amplitudes reduced, velocities relatively preserved (>38 m/s). CMT1: amplitudes reduced AND velocities uniformly very slow (<38 m/s). The prior interpreter focused on the amplitude reduction (consistent with diabetic) without noting the velocity slowing (diagnostic of CMT1).

muscles_tested.morphology: giant polyphasic MUPs — decades of chronic reinnervation

emg.summary: Giant MUPs in multiple muscles indicate decades of chronic denervation-reinnervation since childhood — NOT consistent with 5-year diabetes history. Prior NCS misread: velocity pattern was CMT1, not diabetic axonal.

report.overall_impression: CMT1 HEREDITARY DEMYELINATING NEUROPATHY. Uniformly slow velocities (27-31 m/s throughout), giant MUPs, pes cavus, hammer toes, inverted champagne bottle calves, claw hands, 3-generation family history — CMT1 is the primary diagnosis. Diabetes HbA1c 7.8% contributes superimposed axonal loss but is NOT the primary etiology. GENETIC TESTING: PMP22 duplication (CMT1A) first line; GJB1 (CMTX) if PMP22 negative (X-linked). CIDP excluded by: symmetric, uniform velocities without conduction block, normal CSF (to be obtained), family history.

output.test_type: Focused Wrist NCS — Carpal Tunnel Reassessment

report.summary: FOCUSED CARPAL TUNNEL NCS: Median palmar latency at wrist: 2.0 ms bilaterally. Median-ulnar palmar latency comparison: difference 0.1 ms (both equally slow — because of CMTX global demyelination, not carpal tunnel focal slowing). No median-specific focal slowing at carpal tunnel. Tinel's sign negative bilaterally. CONCLUSION: No carpal tunnel syndrome. Wrist pain was from CMTX-associated hand intrinsic weakness and wrist instability, not carpal tunnel entrapment. Bilateral wrist splints can be discontinued.
report.interpretation: Carpal tunnel syndrome EXCLUDED. Wrist symptoms are from CMTX1 hand weakness (claw hands, intrinsic wasting). The prior carpal tunnel diagnosis was incorrect — typical carpal tunnel shows focal slowing of median nerve at wrist relative to ulnar; in CMTX1, all nerves are equally slow (no focal median slowing at wrist).

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: HbA1c (repeat) 7.6 % (H), eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73m² (H), Urine albumin:creatinine ratio 42 mg/g (H).

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease X-linked type 1 (CMTX1) with superimposed diabetic axonal neuropathy
critical_actions: Re-review prior NCS velocity pattern — uniform slowing <30 m/s is CMT, not diabetic axonal
Obtain 3-generation family history — the 'diabetic neuropathy' label prevented this crucial inquiry
CMT genetic panel (PMP22 then GJB1) — confirm specific type for accurate genetic counseling
CSF protein to exclude CIDP (normal CSF confirms hereditary diagnosis)
Correct carpal tunnel misdiagnosis — wrist splints are unnecessary, important to stop inappropriate intervention
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute to diabetes alone — velocity pattern is diagnostic of hereditary demyelinating neuropathy
Do not prescribe IVIG for CIDP — CMTX1 does not respond to immunotherapy; normal CSF excludes CIDP
Never give vincristine if chemotherapy is required — vincristine causes acute fatal neuropathy in CMT
Do not continue carpal tunnel splints without confirming focal median slowing at wrist

differential.key_distinguishing: HbA1c 7.8% contributes superimposed axonal loss; diabetic neuropathy ALONE does not cause uniformly slow velocities <30 m/s, pes cavus, claw hands, 3-generation family history, or giant MUPs; diabetes is contributing, not primary
PMP22 duplication negative; GJB1 pathogenic variant found — CMTX1, not CMT1A
Normal CSF protein excludes CIDP; uniform symmetric slowing without conduction block or temporal dispersion argues against acquired demyelinating; family history and giant MUPs point to hereditary
Occupational health review negative for toxic exposures; childhood symptoms predated occupation; family history spans 3 generations

key_reasoning_points: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: Three compounding errors led to missed diagnosis — (1) diabetes HbA1c 7.8% caused anchoring, (2) prior NCS misread (amplitude noted, velocity overlooked), (3) family history never obtained
KEY CLUE: Velocity 28-31 m/s throughout all nerves = CMT1 range; diabetic axonal neuropathy shows amplitudes reduced with velocities >38 m/s
GIANT MUPs: Decades of chronic denervation-reinnervation — cannot be explained by 5-year diabetes history; implies childhood-onset neuropathy
PES CAVUS + CLAW HANDS + INVERTED CHAMPAGNE BOTTLE = hereditary neuropathy stigmata; NOT features of diabetic neuropathy
CMTX1 white matter changes on MRI are a distinguishing feature from CMT1A — clinically relevant for counseling about episodic encephalopathy risk
X-LINKED INHERITANCE: Father severely affected (hemizygous male), daughters are obligate carriers, sons of affected father do NOT inherit from father
FALSE CARPAL TUNNEL: Common misdiagnosis in CMT — hand weakness is from intrinsic wasting, not entrapment; NCS shows global slowing without wrist-focal median slowing
